utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Judge. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, please, I have just one question. You described your mission to check the route from Knin to Kijevo, Cetinje, Civljani, Vrlike. And how often did you go and check these villages? Was it several times a day, or was it five or six times in whole? Maybe there was a misunderstanding and we can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My visit to the area, the area that you mentioned, amounted to four or five visits in total, not four or five visits a day. This was, after all, some 50 kilometres from Knin, so we were not able to come back on a daily basis. In addition to that, there were also various checkpoints, and people at those checkpoints wanted to talk to us, and we also attempted to gather as much information as possible when talking to him -- to them. So we had to stay there for quite a while. Therefore, these would be day trips. And we didn't go there every day in a row. We would go there if there was an incident, if something happened there, or when a representative of the Croatian MUP asked us to do that. That's the gentleman under number 10. Or we would go there when the army requested us to go there if there were some conflicts between the citizens and the army. Sometimes Mr. Martic would ask us to go there if there was a conflict involving the Serbian residents in the area. I think that on one occasion I went to the village of Cetinje on a private visit. I was invited to a lunch there. However, things went wrong, and I went back without having eaten lunch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Concerning this list of persons, could you explain once more about the gentleman number 8. Was he a part -- okay. Can we go in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, you mention Knin and a barracks compound and training ground. About how many people in all did you see there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't quite understand the question. Knin, are you referring to the barracks, to the secretariat, or to some other buildings there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry I was not clear. I am referring to the barracks. The compound that you would describe as the training ground.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't referring to the barracks as the place where training was provided. I said that we landed with a helicopter at the barracks, and I went down on two subsequent occasions. But training couldn't be provided in the barracks itself because the barracks was located in the town. There were no grounds that could be used to train the troops, and this is something I could not have seen. They probably had such grounds outside the town. As far as the troops present are concerned, there were very few of them. I asked someone from my area to tell me how many there were there. He said there were very few of us that were allowed in the field, at checkpoints, in the forests, et cetera. Initially he thought that I was asking him how many people from our area, our village, were present there, but that wasn't the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: When he referred to -- when the admiral referred to Captain Dragan, who did you understand him to mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't know his actual real surname for a long time. This was kept secret, perhaps, or perhaps he just wouldn't tell anyone what his surname was. Sometimes such tactics were employed. Only his real name, Kapetan Dragan was used. We found out that he had come from Australia to train special units in the area of SAO Krajina, the Autonomous Region of Krajina. He had come to train Serbian special units. At the time, it was said that Arkan's men were up there, too, but I believe that Arkan was in prison in Zagreb at the time. During that period, he was probably in Zagreb. Perhaps some of Arkan's men or units were down there but not Arkan. However, I can't say anything about this. But as for Kapetan Dragan, Captain Dragan, is concerned, he was in the field down there while we were there, and in conversation this was established, the fact that there was a certain Captain Dragan in the area. And later on I was able to find out that his surname was Vasiljkovic. I don't know how many men there were there, but from the helicopter we could see a certain number of men. I couldn't provide you with an exact number, but there were quite a few people there. The helicopter flew over the area a couple of times, so we could see this. Flew over the fortress a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Please tell me who Arkan is or what were Arkan's units? What's the name of the person, and what did you understand by the term Knindzas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, was a member of some sort of paramilitary units -- or, rather, he was the leader of those paramilitary units, of volunteer paramilitary units. They operated in the territory of Croatia and later on in the territory of Bosnia and in the territory of Kosovo. He had direct control over those volunteers. As far as I'm aware, his command structure was well established, and he kept a tight rein on his troops. On one occasion he got married. I was in Belgrade at the time, and a subordinate of mine went -- a superior of mine went to the -- went to the wedding. I saw this on TV, and a day or two later when I met him, because at the time we had no time constraints, we didn't have to go to work on a daily basis, so when I saw him, I said, "Miljan, you went there too." I was somewhat surprised by his presence at the wedding. And he said, "Well, why not?" That's a private and personal matter. These were informal conversations that we had. And we said that we were a little hurt, affected by the fact that he had gone to his wedding, that he had attended the wedding. And there was another case. Unfortunately this man is no longer alive. It's the son of friend of mine in Belgrade who is concerned. He was a member of Arkan's unit. His mother has died. I don't know whether his father is still alive. His two brothers were killed. On one occasion my wife and I went to pay a visit to the family since we were very close friends. We were good friends with his wife. We were close friends with the mother of that boy who is originally from Kosovo, from Pec. And in terms of culture and mentality, we were identical. But there is an incident that left an impression on me, a lasting impression on me. The mother asked me to try and influence her son Boban, to persuade him not to set off on some sort of adventures. Having spent about five or six minutes in their house, Boban arrived. He was a very fit boy. He trained boxing. I sort of asked him, "What are you doing? How you," et cetera. I said, "I heard that you're going to set off on an adventure," and he said, "Yes, I am." He said, "I'm going to live in Bosnia for a while." I said, "What are you going to do there?" He said, "Well, there are some people that I know that are going to go to that area and try to make a little money." And then he suddenly disappeared for a while. And when he returned, he showed us a lot of gold on -- on some sort of a leather apron. And he offered my wife a sort of necklace that weighed about a kilo. He said, "Here's a present." My wife refused to accept the present. He had a look at me, and I said, "Boban, my wife can't wear this necklace. You didn't buy it. You certainly took it from someone. How did you do?" He said, "That's easy in Bosnia." He said, "If someone doesn't want to take such a necklace off, we cut their head off. If someone doesn't want to take a ring off, we cut the finger off." I said, "Boban, my wife can't and will not wear this." This left a terrible impression on me. It affected me very seriously. I felt sorry for his mother because she was a very decent person. I left the house. I never went there again. I only went there on one other occasion -- I only went to visit her on one other occasion when she was ill in hospital. I later found out that he had been killed. His hands had been tied up, and he was shown on television. (redacted) (redacted) He was shown being buried in a -- in a grave with his hands tied up. Later, his mother told me that he went off with Arkan. But you asked me about Arkan. I think I have been quite clear. Unfortunately, I believe that some people were forced to go to those areas for various reason. It's not as if everyone volunteered, but there were volunteers who acted in such a way to the detriment of other people who belonged to other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And who forced them to go to those various areas for various reasons? [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, probably some sort of an organisation that existed within Arkan's units. I can't provide you with any specific examples, but this is a conclusion that we drew, that we came to when speaking to each other, when I discussed these matters with colleagues. People with criminal backgrounds tended to volunteer. In the case of Boban, his brother had previously been killed in a sports hall in Belgrade. I went to his funeral. And this young man was also well known in the municipality of Palilula for excessive behaviour. Such people participated in such actions. Reasonable people, sane people certainly did not participate in such matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I wonder if out of an abundance of caution we could have a redaction at -- on page 35, line 1 and 2, where the last name of the individual that he was talking about is identified. I think the story without the last name is sufficiently vague, but once the last name is added, it could identify him. So I wonder if that could be redacted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May lines 1 and 2 of page 35 please be deleted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very briefly, what ethnic group did Arkan himself belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was a Serb. I don't know where his mother and father came from. I don't know what their ethnic origin was, but he lived or was born in Slovenia perhaps. I think that's what you could read in the press. I wouldn't go into the details, but he was a Serb. He got married in accordance with Serbian traditions. He was buried. I went to the place where he was buried. I didn't go to his funeral itself, but I did speak to a woman who went to his funeral, and he was buried in accordance with Serbian traditions. He was probably a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: This is my last question to you: You mentioned in relation to a statement made by Mr. Martic that Yugoslavia -- sorry, Yugoslav legislation was of a general nature and it applied to all six republics and the two autonomous provinces and that within that legislative framework each republic adopted its own laws, depending on its own need and requirements, be it the Criminal Code or some other legislation. Now, what I want to ask you: According to how the federal system in Yugoslavia was set up, could one territory try a person for a crime committed in another republic, or did the jurisdiction exist only in the republic where the offence was committed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the Yugoslav law and the law of the other republics, the principles of real and territorial jurisdiction, the principle of subject matter and territorial jurisdiction was applied. This means that the principle of the area where crime was committed applied. Only if the individual concerned had committed crimes on a number of occasions in several republics was there an agreement between the republics according to which one would decide which republic the individual would be tried in. And that was because of territorial jurisdiction and because of subject matter, jurisdiction with regard to the crime and the area where the crime was committed. On the whole, everything was based on the territory in which the crime was committed. Perhaps the lawyers present here could add something to what I have just stated, but I think that in principle this is how things functioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Witness. No further questions from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge. May I just turn your attention to the refugees that you say you saw in the hotel while you were investigating this matter. I know that Mr. Perovic asked you questions about this point in his cross-examination, but I didn't understand your answer and I would like to get clarity on it. He asked you if any houses from where these refugees had been moved were set on fire. I really never got an answer to this question. Were they -- and I'm asking you to please answer very briefly. Don't give me a long story. Were houses in Knin set on fire, houses belongs to those refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my statement, I said that I went to Knin once again. After that, I went to the secretariat building and then went back. That is to say, that I didn't spend much time touring Knin. I think that the gentleman under number 3 and I, I think it was on our way back but I'm not quite sure but it's because it's been a long time, I think that during our trip back we saw one or two houses burning or smouldering. I can't be more specific than that. I can't tell you more about what the refugees said about their houses being set on fire. Some five to six refugees told us that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I'm asking you about observations. Okay? Now, you saw one or two houses smouldering. Did you see any damaged houses as you walked past? I don't think you need to be in the place for too long to observe that. Did you see any damaged buildings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't, because we travelled in a car. So we drove through the area travelling at a speed of 50 to 60 kilometres an hour. So we were unable to observe anything in detail. I saw further away the remains of darkened houses. Now whether those houses had been set on fire a long time before that or just recently, I don't know. But because of the refugees, we sort of paid some attention to that but did not investigate this in-depth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really apologise, but I think we're still in open session, and some of the microphones at the Bench are on, and when the witness is answering with the voice distortion, that causes a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Now, were you travelling through this area in the day or at night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was daylight, as regards that particular day. In general, we tended to travel during daytime, and as soon as the day drew to a close we tended to remain inside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness, you know we do appreciate the detail, but we do have time constraints, and I'm going to ask you to please try to limit yourself only to the questions that I ask. If I need you to give me a fuller explanation, I'll ask for one. And please listen carefully to the question and try to get directly to the answer. Were you aware of any people who may have died during this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean during our mission in Sibenik and Knin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: About how many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One person, a Croat. His name was Vinko Elez. This is what I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And do you know what became of the refugees who were in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We left them at the hotel. They remained there. We went back, and they remained there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You -- are you therefore not able to tell us where they went finally from the hotel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that. Our mission was concluded. We went back, and they remained there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While you were there, for how long did they stay at the hotel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 15 to 20 days. I can't be more specific than that. About 20 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. That's -- any other criminal activity that you may have observed in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Other than that murder with the prisoners, and if we exempt the cases of excessive behaviour on the barricades and the blocking of roads, as far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. In your own judgement, what did you observe the problem to be in this area if you were -- in one sentence were to summarise your observations during that mission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The problem was the co-existence of Serbs and Croats. It was impossible in the area, at least during that period of time. Under the then existing leadership on both sides, it seems to me that the people were heavily manipulated with. They were misdirected by the leadership on both sides. And it was a reflection of the situation in that area, and the same applies to other republics in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just several questions, Your Honours, concerning the questions put by Her Honour Judge Nosworthy to the witness. If we can go into private session, please, just to be on the safe side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution calls its next witness, Witness MM-036. It will be handled by Ms. Richterova, and if Your Honours would permit me to be excused, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are excused, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Shall we move into private session for this witness as he or she comes in?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. May we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, you have been granted certain protective measures in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You will be referred to only by your pseudonym, which means by a number. And also --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Also, your image, when broadcasted, will be distorted so nobody would be able to recognise you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When we are in open session, try to avoid any mentioning of the place you are living or anything which could identify you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If we need to mention such information, then we will go into private session, and I will tell you now you can indicate or you can provide such information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show you a piece of paper. Please have a look and confirm either yes or no, whether it is your name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And if the usher could please show this piece of paper to the Defence counsels and to the Bench. Could this be please admitted into evidence under seal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That document just shown is admitted into evidence under seal. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be exhibit number 284, Your Honours, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we go into private session just for a little while?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, we are now in open session, so please do not mention the name your village. However, I would like to ask you generally. How would you describe the life in -- in your village before the elections, before 1990? How did you get along? How did these two ethnicities get -- got along?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We got along well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you -- so did you socialise together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was there a time when the atmosphere change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell us when was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the voting.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In which way did the atmosphere change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it changed and no one wanted to speak to anyone else any more. Some were for Tudjman and others were for Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In 1991, were you aware of the presence of any armed forces in the area in which you lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who were these armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did JNA -- did JNA come to your village? Did they pass through your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After they had launched rockets, they -- they then passed through.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And before they launch rockets, before this, did JNA pass through your village or were they present in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. They were with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you say they were with the Serbs, do you mean the Serbs in your village or in the other Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were in our village with the Serbs there, and they were in Sladovac.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In Sadilovac, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did Croats in your village, did they have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No weapons whatsoever, or did they have at least some weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they had small quantities of weapons but nothing significant.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did Croats use, in 1991, did they use these weapons against anybody in that region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What about Serbs? Were you aware whether they were armed or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have an objection I would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was whether the Croats were armed and whether the Serbs were armed. This is very general. We can talk about the inhabitants of one village or several villages. Whether the inhabitants were of Croatian nationality or Serbian nationality, and I believe that my colleague should bear this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, I will be more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When I was talking about Croats, I was referring to the village where you lived. Now I'm asking about the Serbs in your village, whether you were aware whether they had any weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you see them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course I saw them. They would bring them in in helicopters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: They -- they brought them with helicopters. When was it? When did you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Where did the helicopter landed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the direction of a place called Duman. That's where they took the weapons, and that's where they hid them too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Richterova, are you rounding your point?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that it's time, and I think that yes, I agree, we can adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If it's convenient. Maybe if you want to round off a point, you can round off the point before we go.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I wanted to ask the question where exactly this place Duman is. Which village is closing to this place, Duman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's near Krslja and Lipovac and Sadilovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's time to take a break. We'll take a short break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, before the break you mentioned a helicopter who landed in -- in the place called Duman. Did you see this helicopter? Did you personally see the helicopter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was there any sign on that helicopter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see that, but it was transporting ammunition and weapons for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said for them. Who did you see to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who did you see together with that helicopter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What kind of troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And where did they take this ammunition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were delivering it to the people. They were arming the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned this presence of JNA. When did they appear in -- in the region, which month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which month? Well, I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Just approximately. Was it spring, summer, autumn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Autumn.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You also mentioned that they launch rockets, and you referred to JNA. Do you remember when this shelling, when was it? When did it take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was sometime in August. Perhaps on the 11th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What kind of weapons did you see with these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer? The interpreter did not hear it clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, would you be so kind and repeat your answer, because the interpreters couldn't follow you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. What would you like me to repeat?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What kind -- what kinds of weapons did these JNA soldiers carry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they had automatic rifles. They had some sort of machine-guns, heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What kind of cars did they have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were in tanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said that they launch these rockets in approximately August. After -- or before August, did you see JNA in tanks passing your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did pass through.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was there any shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Again, repeating this, that they launch rockets, was there any warning which you would receive from any side that -- about the rockets being -- being launched?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was there a time when the JNA would stay in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When did it happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When did it happen? Well, it happened when they entered the village. On that occasion when they were in the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I was more referring to the month.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was around October.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When they entered the village, what happened to the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the civilians fled. Only about 20 of us remained. Between 50 and 20 of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know where the civilian population fled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They fled to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And do you also know why they fled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They fled before the troops, because the war. If they had remained, if they had stayed on, they would all have been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How long this JNA stayed in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, between seven and eight days, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What did they do in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't do anything. They were there and then they set off in the direction of Rakovica to take further territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And after the JNA left the village, what happened? Did anybody else come to the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Paramilitary units arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the army was there, there was a radio post in my house. The army was located in three rooms, and my wife and I were in another room which hadn't been destroyed. The other part had been somewhat destroyed. They would take me to the old house during the day, and in the evening they would come to collect me about half past 7.00 so that I could go to sleep. And then they said, "What are you afraid of?" I said, "I'm not afraid while you are here." They said, "We know. When we leave, beware of the reserve forces of those paramilitary units."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So do you know who were these paramilitary units? Which ethnicity of people they consist of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you know them personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were -- were they from the region or out of the region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were from everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What did they wear? Were they in civilian clothes or in some uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Which uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, like the ones that the army had. Uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what happened after they came to the village? What did they do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did all kinds of things. They set houses on fire, and those who were in the house remained there. That's what they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was anybody killed in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we go, Your Honour, into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we have now reached the portion of your examination called cross-examination. The cross-examination is conducted by the Defence. I am Defence counsel of Milan Martic. I will be putting some questions to you which are of relevance to us. Since you and I understand each other, I will ask you to make pauses between the question and answer so that the interpreters can interpret. Do we understand each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It is stated in your statement that you served your JNA service from 1950 to 1953; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, it also says that you had no schooling prior to the JNA and that you learned to read and write in the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the statement given to the OTP, did you give any other statements to the medical centre or human rights centre in Zagreb? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps give a statement to the medical centre in Slunj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did in Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That was after the events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the statement given to the Prosecution, you spoke about the village where you lived, and you said that there were about 70 houses in there, out of which about 20 were Serbian. Is that what you stated in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement and also today when giving evidence, you said that the relations between the residents of your village were good.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So people got along fine regardless of their ethnicity; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As a turning point in these good relations between the residents, you mentioned the elections in 1990. And my question is: Were these the first multi-party elections in 1990? Do you remember them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that the Croats voted for Tudjman, Serbs for Milosevic, that the Croats wanted Croatia and Serbs wanted Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please wait for me to finish with my question so that the record reflects who puts the question and who provides an answer. So you saw the situation in the elections as follows: The Croats wanted Croatia, and the Serbs wanted, as you just now told us, Krajina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also told us that it was then that you stopped communicating amongst yourselves, the residents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement given to the Prosecutor as well as today in your evidence, you said that the situation in your village was different in May of 1990 precisely because of the elections, that you stopped visiting Serbs in their houses and that the Serbs stopped visiting Croatian houses. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When describing this situation, did you have in mind only your village or neighbouring villages as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's how it was everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that after the elections in 1990 the relations were disrupted, the relations between Serb and Croat residents in many villages and places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your village were there multiple parties? Were there any political parties established before the elections in 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't know whether there were any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the statement given in Karlovac, given to the medical centre there, you described this disruption of communication between the Serbs and Croats, saying that your Serbian best man, this is somebody called kum in your area, and this person, your best man, told you, "Yesterday we used to drink and eat together. Today I no longer know you." Is that what your closest friend, Serb friend, said to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. That's not what he say. And he wasn't my best friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did your kum say that to you? Did your best man say that to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. Somebody else did. He said, "We used to be best men, kums, but we are no longer."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us then, please, what happened in your small village of some 70 houses to make it possible for somebody who were best friends before to stop seeing each other, to stop socialising? You say that you used to be good friends but were no longer friends. What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the politics happened. Though pulled to their side, and we pulled to our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you were pulling to your side. Which side was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What does this mean then, that the Serbs wanted Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the statement given to the OTP, you said that guards were organised in the village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the composition of the population of your village was a mixed one. Croats were a majority and Serbs were the minority. Does this mean that you Croat residents had our own guard duty and that the Serbs had their own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were the Serbian and Croatian houses in your village mixed, or was there one part where there was Serbian houses and another where there were Croatian houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were areas where there were both Serbian and Croatian houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where these guards were mounted, the guards, for example, of the Croats? Did you have checkpoints of any kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was along the road that passed through the village in case troops arrived. That's what the situation was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Which army are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you know which army. The JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that was in May and June 1990, and then we come to 1991. The JNA was the Yugoslav army at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Why did you mount guards in the village along the road in order to spot the rifle of the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this was just a minor action. What can you do if they turn up in tanks if you just have a few rifles?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How far is your village from the Slunj training ground and from Slunj itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 18 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is there a large JNA training ground next to Slunj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is there a permanent troop presence at that training ground? Would that be a regular situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There's a permanent troop presence there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was it quite normal for the troops to pass through the village on their way to the training ground in the state of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it didn't even -- they didn't even pass through our village because that is not the route. It's only when the war broke out that the troops came from up above, from Korenica, Petrovo Selo, and -- and from Sadilovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I wasn't precise enough. Perhaps you could tell us when the war broke out. I assume it was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was it in the summer or the autumn? Could you be more precise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was in the autumn perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you said that the Serbs had split off, had decided to keep themselves apart. You didn't visit each other. You said they even started holding secret meetings. Is that correct? Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that this was the case since you had ceased to visit each other, you had stopped visiting each other? At the end of September or the beginning of October, you said that the JNA took over Lipovaca.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Prior to that event, a day or two earlier, the entire population of the village had fled.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That's what you stated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You served in the military. As we can see, you know what regular troops are. You know what reserve forces are. Can you distinguish between the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can, and I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That day when, as you say, the JNA entered the village, were the troops regular JNA troops? They were regular JNA units, is that what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were regular troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe the sort of uniforms these troops who entered your village were wearing? And you said that they even stayed in your house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: My question was whether you could describe the uniforms they were wearing. Were they wearing olive-drab uniforms or camouflage ones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, camouflage ones. In fact, they had camouflage uniforms and other kinds of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When describing that seven- or eight-day period during which the JNA was present in your village, you said that on one day you spoke to a JNA soldier who asked you whether you were afraid.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And you told him that for as long as they were there you were not afraid; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you believed that for as long as the JNA troops were there no harm would come to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you then tell us why the inhabitants of the village fled from the village before the JNA troops arrived? Why were they afraid? Who had scared them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were afraid of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In 1991 -- before the summer of 1991, Croatia had declared that it would be seceding for Yugoslavia. When the JNA entered your village at that time, did Croatia have an army of its own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the name of that Croatian army was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What was its name?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was it the ZNG, the National Guards, or some other name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was some sort of a MUP force, Ministry of the Interior force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This MUP force, were they part of the Croatian Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's quite certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where were these MUP forces deployed? Were they in village, and were they present in the surrounding Croatian villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were very few of them. Some of them were in Rakovica and in Slunj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that there were such Croatian forces in Dreznik, Rakovica, and Slunj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And you said there were very few of them. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were very few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean there were very few of them because they couldn't confront the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, they couldn't. This army was the third greatest force in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the army, the JNA, arrived in your village, stayed there seven or eight days, and you saw that they were shelling Rakovica and Dreznik town.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the JNA open fire on Croatian policemen there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had already left by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I didn't understand you correctly. You answered my question while I was still speaking. Could you just repeat your answer, please? Did the JNA open fire on Croatian policemen in Dreznik and Rakovica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How far is Dreznik town from your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were you by the JNA tanks when they opened fire on the town of Dreznik? Were you at home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they took Dreznik when they were leaving Korenica and going to Petrovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you weren't by the tanks when they opened fire but the tanks were by your house. Were you in the cellar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They opened fire from in front of our house on the church, but there was no one there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how could you have seen this? How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were in front of my house. How could I fail to see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: From a distance of three kilometres, they opened fire from tanks on the church?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that the range of a tank gun is two and a half kilometres, maximum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How would I know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned some JNA helicopter. You didn't see any marks on the helicopter, but you believe it was a military one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was a military helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question from the Prosecution, you said that the helicopter landed in some village somewhere. Can you repeat the name of the village and tell us how far it is from your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It headed in the direction of Duman. It's a small place. And they were transporting goods and ammunition there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were you in the place where the helicopter landed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, on what basis can you claim that the helicopter was transporting what you say it was transporting? How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, other people who had seen the helicopter told me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'll rephrase this question. You heard from others that the troops were using a helicopter to transport weapons and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's what they were transporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And you said, in response to a question from the Prosecution, that the troops was transporting ammunition and weapons in this helicopter for itself, too, and they probably provided the Serbs with these goods.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So could we say that you have no direct information about all of these events? What you have told us is hearsay; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you mentioned the territorial units, you said that: "The JNA stayed in our village for seven or eight days. When they left, several of us who had remained in the village were afraid and we all fled to the forest and spent the night there." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that later on some armed individuals arrived in the village. You said that these were members of paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who were these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were called Martic's troops, Martic's army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What is a paramilitary unit, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we called them reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So you are now saying that you called them reserve forces. Do you mean the reserve forces of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you said the Territorial Defence. Are you referring to the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you did not know those men, but do you have any ideas as to their identity? Were they from the surroundings? Who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, how would I know? I wouldn't have known anything if there hadn't been that radio post in our house. The young men said, "For as long as we are here, you have nothing to worry about. When we leave, beware of the reserve forces." They would beat the people, set houses on fire, loot, et cetera. Whoever stayed on would be killed, regardless of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions. This concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I would have one question concerning these helicopters. You, first to the Prosecution, said that there would be helicopters - that means not only one helicopter but more than one - and you saw them. And now concerning the question what the helicopters have transported, you then made that point that this is not your own view. You had only heard of that. So I would like to know what did you see yourself, and what did you hear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm not sure if I understand you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you carry on, I see we are in open session and we are mentioning names of places. Shall we perhaps go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. And just to be on the safe side, I would ask to redact page 28 from line 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we please delete page 28 from line 23 to the end of that, and possibly the first line of page 29.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: First three lines, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: First three lines of page 29. And then after that, may we please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It's the end for us today. The next witness will be called by Colin Black tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That being the case, we are going to adjourn until tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in Courtroom I. Courtroom I, quarter past 2.00 tomorrow. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 5th day of April, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 22 23 24 25
